web.title: arXiv:1802.08667v5  [stat.ML]  13 Apr 2021
web.description:
We construct a Neyman orthogonal equation for
the target parameter that is approximately invariant to small perturbations of the nui-
sance parameters. To achieve this property, we include the Riesz representer for the
functional as an additional nuisance parameter. Our analysis yields weak “double spar-
sity robustness”: either the approximation to the regression or the approximation to
the representer can be “completely dense” as long as the other is sufficiently “sparse”.
Our main results are non-asymptotic and imply asymptotic uniform validity over large
classes of models, translating into honest confidence bands for both global and local
parameters.

To avoid such bias, we use debiased/“double” ma-
chine learning (DML) based on Neyman orthogonal scores that have zero derivative with
respect to each first step learner (e.g., Neyman (1959); Belloni et al. (2014, 2015); Cher-
nozhukov et al. (2016, 2018); Foster and Syrgkanis (2019)). Note that the word “double”
emphasizes the connection to double robustness, a property which orthogonal scores have
in this case. Such scores are constructed by adding a bias correction term: the average
product of the regression residual with a learner of the functional’s Riesz representer
(RR).

web.title: De-Biased Machine Learning of Global and Local Parameters Using Regularized Riesz Representers
web.description:
To avoid such bias, we use debiased/“double” machine learning (DML) based on Neyman orthogonal scores that have zero derivative with respect to each first step learner (e.g., Neyman 1959; Belloni et al. 2014; Belloni et al. 2015; Chernozhukov et al. 2016; Chernozhukov et al. 2018a; Foster and Syrgkanis 2019). Note that the word “double” emphasizes the connection to double robustness, a property which orthogonal scores have in this case. Such scores are constructed by adding a bias correction term: the average product of the regression residual with a learner of the functional’s Riesz representer (RR).

The Neyman orthogonality property states that the representation of the target parameter in terms of the nuisance parameters is invariant to the local perturbations of the values of the nuisance parameter. This property makes the orthogonal representation an excellent basis for constructing high quality point and interval estimators of in modern high-dimensional settings when we will be plugging-in biased estimators in lieu of and , where the bias occurs because of the regularization (see, e.g., Chernozhukov et al. 2016; Chernozhukov et al. 2018a).

web.title: Ill-Conditioned Orthogonal Scores in Double Machine Learning
web.description:
Double Machine Learning (DML; Chernozhukov et al.,, [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib5)) permits the application of machine learning methods for nuisance estimation, while preserving $\sqrt{n}$-inference for low-dimensional treatment effects. This holds because Neyman-orthogonal scores reduce first-order sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and cross-fitting avoids own-observation bias (Chernozhukov et al.,, [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib5); Kennedy,, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib20)). As a result, the corresponding sufficient conditions are typically stated as rate conditions, rather than as parametric smoothness restrictions. In the canonical partially linear regression (PLR) model, for instance, the classical product-rate requirement is $r_{n}^{m}r_{n}^{\ell}=o_{P}(n^{-1/2})$, where $r_{n}^{m},r_{n}^{\ell}$ denote $L^{2}$ nuisance-estimation rates (Chernozhukov et al.,, [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib5)).

Two theoretical connections improve interpretation. First, we link conditioning to semiparametric efficiency geometry by proving $\kappa=\sigma_{D}^{2}\|\alpha_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}$, where $\alpha_{0}$ is the Riesz representer (Chernozhukov et al.,, [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib7)). Second, we formalize weakening overlap through a triangular-array framework in which $\kappa_{n}\to\infty$.

The estimand $\theta_{0}$ is causal under standard potential-outcome conditions: consistency ($Y=Y(D)$), conditional exogeneity ($\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid D,X]=0$), and overlap ($\mathrm{Var}(D\mid X)>0$). In the PLR framework, these conditions imply the orthogonal moment $\mathbb{E}[V\cdot(Y-g_{0}(X)-\theta_{0}(D-m_{0}(X)))]=0$ (Chernozhukov et al.,, [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib5)).

###### Lemma 3.4 (Neyman Orthogonality).
The pathwise derivative of $\mathbb{E}[\psi(W;\theta_{0},\eta)]$ with respect to $\eta$ vanishes at $\eta_{0}$. This property is the cornerstone of debiased machine learning (Chernozhukov et al.,, [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib5)).
The proof is in Appendix A.2. Neyman orthogonality implies the first-order effect of nuisance perturbations on the population moment vanishes. Combined with cross-fitting, the leading sample terms involving $\Delta^{m},\Delta^{\ell}$ are mean-zero and of order $(r_{n}^{m}+r_{n}^{\ell})/\sqrt{n}$, while the systematic remainder is second order (e.g., $r_{n}^{m}r_{n}^{\ell}$ and $(r_{n}^{m})^{2}$).

This is the Riesz representer for the functional $\theta\mapsto\mathbb{E}[\alpha(W)\cdot\theta D]$ restricted to the space orthogonal to $L^{2}(P_{X})$, expressed as a constrained minimal-norm problem (Chernozhukov et al.,, [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib7)).

Theorem [3.6](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#S3.Thmtheorem6) grounds our diagnostic in modern semiparametric theory (Newey,, [1990](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib25); Kennedy,, [2016](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib19); Chernozhukov et al.,, [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.07083v2#bib.bib7)). The minimal-norm representer $\alpha_{0}$ is the correction weight for double robustness. Its norm measures how much correction is required. A large $\|\alpha_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}$ signals both large variance and large sensitivity to nuisance bias.

web.title: Improved methods of combining forecasts - Granger - 1984 - Journal of Forecasting - Wiley Online Library
web.description: First published: April/June 1984 ... It is well known that a linear combination of forecasts can outperform individual forecasts. The common practice, however, is to obtain a weighted average of forecasts, with the weights adding up to unity. This paper considers three alternative approaches to obtaining linear combinations. It is shown that the best method is to add a constant term and not to constrain the weights to add to unity. These methods are tested with data on forecasts of quarterly hog prices, both within and out of sample. It is demonstrated that the optimum method proposed here is superior to the common practice of letting the weights add up to one.
